references.text: Matthew's parallel account of the officer's servant who was sick. Here the officer himself comes to Jesus and tells him that the servant is lying at home paralyzed and suffering terribly.
The conclusion of the parallel account in Matthew, where Jesus heals the servant's illness from a distance.
A royal official in Capernaum whose son was near death, a similar situation where a person in authority seeks Jesus for healing of someone close to dying.
Jesus heals the royal official's son from a distance, just as the officer's servant in Luke 7 was also healed from a distance.

The continuation of the account shows that the officer sent Jewish elders to Jesus, and they testified that he was worthy because he loved the Jewish people and had built the synagogue – which emphasizes that the servant was precious to him (ἔντιμος).

Cornelius, another Roman officer (ἑκατοντάρχης), who was also devout and God-fearing, and who sought contact with God's people – a parallel to the officer in Luke 7 who valued his servant and the Jewish people.
Paul urges masters to treat their slaves justly, which reflects the care the officer in Luke 7:2 showed for his servant who was precious to him.
Jesus commends the officer's faith as greater than any he has found in Israel, and when the messengers returned, they found the servant well – the outcome of the account that begins in verse 2.
